title: Aurora Health - POC quality evaluation scoping
summary: POC scoping focused on quality-eval plan for clinical note generation and triage assistant: define golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination checks, structural/format validations, scoring methodology and workload sizing for benchmarks. Agreed on a 10k prompt pilot, success criteria thresholds, and immediate next steps to share eval template and schedule benchmark kickoff.
next_steps: Redwood to send eval template + golden prompt spreadsheet (Maya) - due 2025-03-06
Customer to provide 2k sample prompts and schema examples (Priya) - due 2025-03-10
Schedule benchmark kickoff call w/ infra (week of 2025-03-17) (Daniel + Carlos)
Run smoke benchmarks (1k prompts) then full benchmark (10k prompts) - target complete by 2025-03-28
action_items: Maya: share quality-eval template and scoring rubric - 2025-03-06
Priya: export 2,000 de-identified sample prompts + desired output schema - 2025-03-10
Daniel & Carlos: validate VPC egress rules and provide access method (SFTP vs presigned URL) - 2025-03-12
Leah: confirm stakeholders for final review and legal contact for data use - 2025-03-07
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we should have about an hour. I'm Maya, AE on the account, Daniel from our SE team is here to run through the eval plan.
[00:12] Priya Rao: Hi, thanks. I have Leah and Carlos on. We're excited but also pretty strict about hallucinations in clinical notes so need to scope that.
[00:20] Daniel Kim: Cool, quick agenda — golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination/format checks, scoring approach, and benchmark sizing/timing.
[00:31] Carlos Mendez: Quick infra note, we'll need to know whether you're pulling logs or pushing results, our security team prefers SFTP or presigned URLs.
[00:40] Maya Patel: Yep noted Carlos, we'll include both.
[00:45] Priya Rao: For context, our POC goal is to replace a portion of the manual triage summaries with model-generated summaries — must keep PHI scrubbed, zero actionable hallucinations, and maintain specific JSON schema for downstream systems.
[00:58] Daniel Kim: Understood. On the eval side we typically do: 1) golden prompts (a small curated set with gold outputs), 2) a regression test harness where we compare new model outputs to previous baseline, 3) hallucination detection checks (entity hallucination, unsupported assertions), and 4) structural/format validation.
[01:15] Leah O'Connor: Walk me through the golden prompts — how many do you usually use?
[01:21] Daniel Kim: We recommend 100-300 high-coverage golden prompts covering critical edge cases. The golden set is hand-labeled by your SMEs so we know what a correct clinical summary looks like. It helps us calibrate automatic metrics and set thresholds.
[01:34] Priya Rao: 300 seems high — our SME time is limited. Can we do 150?
[01:40] Maya Patel: 150 is fine as a starting point, we can prioritize by risk area. We'll ask for annotator notes with each golden sample.
[01:47] [01:50] Speaker 3: (unclear) — sorry, dropped for a sec.
[01:56] Daniel Kim: On metrics, we'll run both automatic and human-in-the-loop scoring. Automatic: ROUGE-L for content overlap, a custom hallucination detector (entity mismatch rate), and structural pass-rate for JSON schema. Human scoring: binary correctness on critical facts, and a 0-3 severity for hallucinated assertions.
[02:18] Carlos Mendez: How do you define hallucination here? For example if the model adds a medication not in the note — that's immediate fail?
[02:26] Daniel Kim: Yes — adding new medications or dosages is a high-severity hallucination. We mark that as a critical fail during the golden set evaluation. Lower severity would be stylistic embellishments not changing clinical action.
[02:36] Priya Rao: What about partial matches, like model paraphrases a symptom but misses onset timing — how do we score that?
[02:42] Daniel Kim: For onset timing we treat it as a fact — human labelers will mark missing or incorrect timing as a defect. In automatic scoring we try to extract entities (Symptom, Onset, Med) and compute precision/recall on those fields to approximate missing info.
[02:55] Maya Patel: For success criteria our typical thresholds for a production pilot are: golden set pass >= 92% (weighted by critical facts), hallucination rate <= 0.5% for critical entities, and structural schema pass-rate >= 98%. Those are starting points; we can negotiate depending on your risk tolerance.
[03:15] Priya Rao: 92% is ambitious but acceptable for a pilot if the hallucination rate is low. For PHI scrubbing we have to ensure no raw PHI is exposed during the benchmark. We'll only share de-identified examples.
[03:29] Daniel Kim: Good point — we'll accept de-identified prompts. For post-benchmark logs, we can provide redacted token-level logs or aggregated metrics per your compliance needs.
[03:40] Leah O'Connor: Timeline? How long would a full benchmark take?
[03:45] Daniel Kim: Operationally we do a 1k smoke run to validate setup (a day), and then a 10k full-run which depending on concurrency and model size can take 2-4 days for generation plus 3-5 days for human review and scoring. So overall 1-2 weeks from kickoff.
[03:59] Carlos Mendez: For workload sizing — what concurrency and token rates should we expect? Our triage notes average 450 tokens per prompt and outputs average ~220 tokens.
[04:09] Daniel Kim: Thanks, that's great. For 10k prompts at average 220 tokens output and 450 input, total token volume is roughly 6.7M tokens. If you want a baseline latency SLO of 700ms p50 and 1.4s p95 for interactive triage, we recommend running benchmarks at 30–50 qps (we'll size GPU accordingly). For throughput-focused bench we can compress to batch mode and measure tokens per second.
[04:32] Priya Rao: We care more about p95 latency than raw throughput.
[04:36] Maya Patel: We'll include both latency and cost columns in the bench spreadsheet so you can see tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated vs quantized variants.
[04:45] [04:47] Speaker 2: (murmur)
[04:50] Daniel Kim: Regression testing — we maintain a baseline model run (your current on-prem or a chosen open-variant). For each run we compute delta metrics: decrease in correct facts, change in hallucination rate, and the cost delta. We flag regressions beyond a configurable tolerance (e.g., >2% drop on critical facts).
[05:07] Priya Rao: Our baseline currently is a tuned open model, not Redwood's endpoint. Can you run comparative bench against our baseline?
[05:13] Daniel Kim: Yes, we can run side-by-side comparisons. We'll need your baseline model outputs for the golden prompts or we can run them ourselves if you grant access.
[05:22] Leah O'Connor: Structural/format checks — we can't have malformed JSON hitting downstream processors.
[05:27] Daniel Kim: Absolutely. We run schema validation on every output. We'll report schema pass-rate and examples of failures. In the POC we'll include automated fix suggestions when feasible, e.g., attempt to coerce fields into types, otherwise mark as fail.
[05:40] Carlos Mendez: Any tools for hallucination detection you use? Off-the-shelf or custom?
[05:44] Daniel Kim: We use a mix. For entity hallucination we run an entity-extraction model plus fuzzy matching to source text. For assertion-level hallucination we run entailment or QA checks against the source text. It's not perfect — that's why human review remains part of the loop.
[05:58] Priya Rao: Scoring rubric detail please — how are weights assigned between structural, hallucination, and content accuracy?
[06:05] Daniel Kim: Typical weight: critical facts (entities like meds, dosages, allergies) 50%, hallucination penalty 30% (counts negative), structural/schema 10%, fluency/readability 10% for human scoring. We can adjust weights — for you we should probably give extra weight to hallucination penalty and schema.
[06:23] Maya Patel: Let's annotate that as a change: weight critical facts 55%, hallucination penalty 35%, schema 10%. We'll reflect that in the rubric.
[06:30] Priya Rao: Good. On timelines for human review, do you source reviewers or do we provide SMEs?
[06:36] Maya Patel: We can support initial human scoring to accelerate, but for final accept/reject we ask that your SMEs sign off on golden set and some sampled reviews. We'll propose a blended approach: Redwood does bulk labeling via contractor vetters for speed, and Aurora SMEs spot-check.
[06:49] Leah O'Connor: Budget question — do human reviews cost extra?
[06:53] Maya Patel: Yes, we itemize review hours in the POC cost estimate. We'll include estimates for SME time vs contractor labeling.
[06:59] [07:01] Speaker 3: (background noise)
[07:05] Daniel Kim: Another instrumentation detail: we include token-level latency histograms, per-prompt trace IDs you can correlate back to raw input, and a per-route cost estimate. For private deployment options we can run bench inside your VPC to avoid egress.
[07:20] Carlos Mendez: We'll prefer VPC bench.
[07:23] Daniel Kim: Noted. For data movement we'll support presigned S3 URLs or a Snowball-type transfer if needed — but presigned URLs are easiest for a 10k prompt run.
[07:33] Priya Rao: On hallucination thresholds, you mentioned 0.5% for critical entities. Is that per-prompt or per-field?
[07:40] Daniel Kim: It's per critical-entity occurrence across the dataset. We'll surface both per-prompt and per-field rates.
[07:47] Maya Patel: Quick operational checklist to kick off: 1) Aurora provides de-identified 2k sample + schema and SME contacts, 2) Redwood shares golden-prompt template & rubric, 3) decide on bench location (hosted vs VPC), 4) schedule kickoff.
[08:05] Leah O'Connor: Can we do an initial smoke run next Wednesday?
[08:09] Daniel Kim: Yes, if we get the 1k sample and access by Monday we can.
[08:14] Priya Rao: We'll aim to provide the 2k sample by Monday EOD.
[08:19] Maya Patel: Great — I'll send the template after this call. Any other questions?
[08:24] Carlos Mendez: One more — how do you handle update rollouts if a model regresses in production?
[08:29] Daniel Kim: We maintain rollback policies and can configure canary rollouts with traffic split and automated regression monitors. If a regression is detected, we have automated fallback to baseline model and alerting.
[08:41] Leah O'Connor: Perfect.
[08:44] Maya Patel: Awesome — recap of next steps and owners in chat. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials.
[08:52] Priya Rao: Thanks all.
[08:55] [END]
questions: How many golden prompts are needed?
notes: Preference for VPC presigned URL transfer
